entry.summary: Most organizations exploring AI already have an application that works. It supports daily operations, holds years of business data, and is familiar to the people who use it. The question is rarely whether to replace that application. It is whether AI can make it more useful without disrupting what already runs. There is a common assumption that adding AI requires a new platform, a new architecture, or a rebuild of the existing system. In most cases it does not. For the majority of business use cases, AI is added the same way other capabilities have always been added: as a new feature that uses an external service. entry.title: Realtime Event Retention Policy: Scaling Delivery Tracking Maps Through 3 Recovery Windows
entry.summary:
Short answer: keep a short, lossless stream for reconnects, a compact snapshot for backfill, and discard movement noise once the map has caught up. That split scales realtime event delivery without pretending a tracking map needs an eternal event log. The awkward part is choosing the boundary. A courier's typing indicator (the dispatcher is composing a note) wants seconds of retention. A read receipt wants a durable state transition. A GPS marker wants the newest position, not every point recorded while a phone was underground. Treating all three as “events” is how a small map turns into a replay bill and a slow reconnect path.

entry.title: Kubernetes Resource Requests and Limits (2026): Set Them Right and Prevent OOMKilled & FailedScheduling
entry.summary:
TL;DR
Requests are what the scheduler spends; limits are what the kernel enforces. A pod is placed based on its requests, and killed or throttled based on its limits. CPU and memory fail differently: exceed your CPU limit and you get throttled (slow); exceed your memory limit and you get killed (OOMKilled, exit code 137). Two of the most common Kubernetes errors are born here: FailedScheduling (requests too big to place) and OOMKilled (memory limit set from hope). Both are manifest bugs, not cluster bugs. Set values from measurement, not vibes: observe real usage over at least one full traffic cycle, set requests near typical peak, give memory a limit with honest headroom. Every container needs both numbers, including sidecars and init containers — the one you skip is the one that gets…

entry.title: Halloween Dev Horror: 5 micro stories with protective charms
entry.summary: Happy Halloween. Scarier than ghost stories: 5 micro horror stories that could actually happen. Three sentences each. Night 1, "The Window": Two terminals open — staging and production. You hit Enter. Then you read the window title. Charm: color-code production; double-confirm dangerous commands. Night 2, "The Space": You meant to delete ./build. You typed rm -rf . /build. Charm: ls first to see what you're deleting; protect and back up key directories. Night 3, "The Backup": Every night, the backup said "success". Then you needed to restore. The files were empty. Charm: a backup only counts if you can restore it — practice. In 2017 GitLab accidentally deleted a production database, several backup methods failed, and about 6 hours of data was lost; their public post-mortem is still required reading. Night 4, "The Key": 3 a.m., a cloud billing alert with extra zeros. You remember the config file you pushed to a public repo yesterday. Charm: scan commits for secrets; if leaked, revoke and regenerate immediately. Night 5, "Friday": 5 p.m. Friday. "It's one line, quick deploy." Charm: …just don't. 3 everyday guardrails: preview before you run anything dangerous; actually restore a backup now and then; keep keys out of repos. When AI can run commands for you, install guardrails first: BFBT Code's Hooks can require checks before risky steps, and DTworkeasy lets you stop things from your phone. Which story gave you chills? Got one of your own?
